\subsection{Prescriptive Framework}\label{sec:selection_method}

The diagnostic analysis identifies two necessary conditions for LP selection to improve over greedy decoding: (1)~low instance degeneracy and (2)~adequate within-instance LP-quality alignment ($\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$).
We formalize these as a practitioner checklist: compute dataset-level degeneracy and within-instance $\rho$; apply LP selection only when both conditions are met, defaulting to greedy otherwise.
Unlike adaptive SC methods that gate on answer agreement \cite{aggarwal2023adaptive} or response confidence \cite{kim2026reasc}, these conditions are specific to structured prediction where identical entity sets yield identical F1.

\paragraph{Controlled validation (DGS).}
To test whether the framework's predictions are accurate, we implement degeneracy-gated selection (DGS): for each instance, LP selects among $N$ candidates if the within-instance LP range exceeds the dataset-specific median; otherwise, greedy output is retained.
%% TODO: DGS threshold details may be refined after gold-filter rerun
DGS serves as a controlled experiment: if the two-condition framework is correct, DGS should yield gains where both conditions hold (Few-NERD) and fail where either is violated (CoNLL, SciERC).

The diagnostic analysis identifies two necessary conditions for LP selection to improve over greedy decoding: (1)~low instance degeneracy and (2)~adequate within-instance LP-quality alignment ($\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$).
We formalize these as a practitioner checklist: compute dataset-level degeneracy and within-instance $\rho$; apply LP selection only when both conditions are met, defaulting to greedy otherwise.
Unlike adaptive SC methods that gate on answer agreement \cite{aggarwal2023adaptive} or response confidence \cite{kim2026reasc}, these conditions are specific to structured prediction where identical entity sets yield identical F1.

\paragraph{Controlled validation.}
We validate the framework with degeneracy-gated selection (DGS): LP selects among $N$ candidates if within-instance LP range exceeds the dataset-specific median; otherwise, greedy output is retained.

1	\begin{abstract}
2	Self-consistency yields large gains on discrete-answer tasks, but named entity recognition (NER) produces \textit{sets} of entities with partial overlap, where no majority vote analog exists.
3	We evaluate five confidence signals (four instance-level, one per-sample log-probability [LP]) for quality estimation and sample selection on four NER benchmarks using 4B\textendash 8B models.
4	All signals achieve reliable quality estimation, supporting selective prediction.
5	For selection, LP achieves $+1.39$~pp on Few-NERD in settings where both low instance degeneracy and adequate LP-quality alignment are present.
6	When either factor is absent, LP gains fall below detectable thresholds despite ${\sim}$13~pp oracle headroom, a disparity we term the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}.
7	Two mechanisms explain this gap: \textit{instance degeneracy} (14\textendash 59\% of instances yield identical F1 scores across all samples) eliminates headroom; \textit{weak LP-quality alignment} prevents exploiting the remainder.
8	Degeneracy is controllable via temperature and training convergence; neither scalar signal combinations nor learned text representations close the gap.
9	Hidden state probes confirm information beyond LP exists in model representations, but the correlation-selection gap persists: richer signals do not improve selection in the high-capability regime.
10	\end{abstract}
